newsitem.title: UK: LME nickel hits two-year lows, copper off highs.
newsitem.headline: LME nickel hits two-year lows, copper off highs.

text.p: Nickel prices slumped to two-year lows on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Monday, driven down by speculative chart-based sales and weak fundamentals.
Copper rose to a five-month peak early in the day before profit-taking pared almost all of the day's gains.
Other base metals were down slightly from Friday.
Three month nickel futures finished the afternoon kerb trading session at $6,620 a tonne, down $430 or over six percent, from Friday's finish.
The market fell to $6,600 at one stage, the lowest level seen since October 1994.
"This isn't really news-driven. Someone had nickel to sell early, and when the market got below $7,000 chart-based selling was triggered," said one nickel trader.
"We heard the funds were selling it early this morning and that appears to have carried on throughout the day," another trader added.
Weak fundamentals have also been undermining prices for some time, the dealers added.
LME stocks have risen steadily in the last few months while inventories of Russian nickel in Europe and a worldwide overhang of stainless steel scrap have hit primary nickel demand.
Copper moved in the opposite direction early on as short-covering sent three month values to a peak of $2,198, the highest level for five months.
Spreads also flared, with cash/threes hitting $130 backwardation at one stage.
But profit-taking helped pare the gains and three months finished the afternoon kerb just $11 higher at $2,159. Cash/threes was last indicated at around $115 backwardation.
Some traders said an investment bank could be capping the market in order to protect substantial short call option positions at around $2,300.
Influential fund shorts had also been covering substantial tonnages during the last few trading days, traders said.
LME stocks were expected to fall on Tuesday, with one dealer pegging the expected drawdown at around 4,000 tonnes.
This would take total LME copper stocks to below 100,000 tonnes. Inventories already stand at six-year lows.

Traders said the widening backwardation may attract more metal on to the exchange, but some Asian dealers said China may be taking more copper into its own state reserve than originally expected, possibly to feed big infrastructure projects.
Other base metals were relatively stable.
Aluminium edged back $6.50 to $1,434.50 while zinc fell $6 to $1,058.
Tin dropped $30 to $6,030 and lead eased $7.50 to $717.50.
Alloy was last indicated at $1,300/05 against $1,295 on Friday.
--Mike Collett-White, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8057
